name: Mary
whenBasis: From the annunciation, before Herod's death in 4 BC, to her presence with the disciples in Jerusalem after the ascension (Acts 1:14).
summary: A young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, to whom the angel Gabriel announced that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son named Jesus. She answered, “I am the Lord's servant,” visited her relative Elizabeth, and sang the Magnificat. She gave birth in Bethlehem, fled with Joseph and the child to Egypt, and raised him in Nazareth. At Cana she told the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.” She stood by the cross, where Jesus gave her to the disciple he loved, and prayed with the disciples after the ascension.
body: Luke twice says she treasured up what happened and pondered it in her heart. Simeon tells her a sword will pierce her soul. When the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in the temple, she says, “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.”

Once during the ministry she and his brothers come to take him home, and he answers that whoever does the will of God is his mother and brothers. Mark and Matthew name the brothers James, Joses or Joseph, Judas and Simon, and mention sisters.

moments.text: A sword will pierce your soul

later.text: The Protevangelium of James, from the second century, names her parents Joachim and Anna and tells of her childhood in the temple.
traditions: the Protevangelium of James, and Catholic and Orthodox tradition after it

later.text: The Council of Ephesus (431) called her Theotokos, God-bearer. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that she remained a virgin; Catholics also define her Immaculate Conception (1854) and Assumption (1950), and Orthodox Christians keep her Dormition.

Jesus' brothers and sisters have been read as Mary's later children (Helvidius, and most Protestants today), Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (Epiphanius, and the Orthodox), or cousins (Jerome, and Catholic tradition).
